Buenos Aires, Oct. 1 ()-—Argen-|~ 
tina announced today she had ad- 
justed her peso rates in view of 
ithe devaluations of currencies 
throughout the world touched off 
by Britain's cheapening of her? 
money. 
The Argentine Government 
Vcreased the value of the peso 
relation to the pound, but some 
rates for the peso were devalued 
‘in relation to the dollar. 
9 Apparently, this was an attempt 
to compel Britain to pay more of 
her devalued pounds for her meat 
Jsupplies from Argentina and at the 
same time stimulate sales of Argen- 
tine goods in the United Siates and | 
jmake up for a serious shortage of | 


The government issued an elabo- 
rate new table of exchange rates, 
but left for next week the explana- 
tion of how these rates will apply 
to the nation’s exports and imports. 
Before September 19, the so-called 
free rate of the Argentine peso was 
54.875 to the dollar. 

Today’s announcement did not} 
Visay what the new free rate would! 
ibe, but Alfredo Gomez Morales, 
finance minister, said it would be | 
“stimulated.” Private bankers said 
this meant devaluation in relation | 
to the dollar.

/ing on the black market here for 
g 2s high as 13 pesos, which made the

jrent “free rate.” The so-called free 
jrates apply on transfers of money 
for services, travel and profits. 

Different Scales Maintained 

On imports and exports Argen- 
jtina maintains a scale of rates: for 
selling products hard to sell and 
\for buying necessities, the peso 
trate is low; for selling products 
like grains, which find ready buy- 
iers, and for imports of luxuries, 
like automobiles, the rate is high. 

Heretofore, the highest rate on 
jexports was 5 pesos to the dollar. 
|The new list today shows a special 
jrate as high as 7.1964.

‘paid for meat had been converted 
at the rate of 13.53 pesos. Today’s 
table contains a new rate: 9.40 
pesos. Presumably this is intended 
|to apply to meat sales, since it is

SUFFICIENTLY TO CHANGE HIS MIND. 

"THERE IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR DIRECT, FREE DEALS BETWEEN PRIVATE 
BUYERS AND SELLERS AND THE ONLY REAL WAY TO RESTORE TRADE IS TO 
RESTORE SUCH DEALS. ITIL THE JAPANESE HAVE TRADING RIGHTS AND 
CONSULAR SERVICES ABROAD, FOREIGN TRADERS IN JAPAN SHOULD BE EN- 
COURAGED TO DO BUSINESS FREELY. THEY SHOULD NOT BE BOUND UP IN 
REAMS OF RED TAPE. AND ONCE THE JAPANESE MERCHANTS REGAIN THEIR 
TRADING RIGHTS AND CONSULAR SERVICES THEY SHOULD BE GIVEN BACK THEIR 
GLADSTONE BAGS AND SENT OUT ON THE ROAD,

“NEW YORK, OCT.2- =(AP)= -RANDOLFO PACCIARD1y “ITALIAN MINISTER 
DEFENSE, SAID TODAY HE DID NOT BELIEVE THE WESTERN POWERS WOULD 
ABANDON ITALY IN-CASE OF AN ATTACK FROM THE EAST. 

PACCIARDI WAS ASKED BY NEWSMEN ABOUT REPORTSTHAT ATLANTIC PACT 
STRATEGISTS, IN THE EVENT OF SUCH AN ATTACK, MIGHT ESTABLISH A DEFENSE | 
LINE IN THE ALPS BETWEEN ITALY AND FRANCE. SUCH A LINE WOULD LEAVE 
ITALY ONLY PARTIALLY PROTECTED. 

THE ITALIAN MINISTER, WHO ARRIVED BY PLANE TO TAKE PART IN 
a PACT DEFENSE COMMITTEE TALKS OPENING WEDNESDAY IN WASHINGTON, 

"WE CANNOT CONSIDER THE POSSIBILITY OF THE ABANDONMENT OF ITALY IN 
CASE OF ATTACK FROM THE EAST. THAT IS NOT ONLY MY OPINION BUT ALSO 
THE ITALIAN PEOPLE." 

HE SAID ITALY WOULD PREPARE ITS PEACETIME DEFENSES WITHIN ‘THE 
LIMITS IMPOSED BY ITS PEACE TREATY.

Canton. China, Oct. 3 (4)—The} 
Nationalist Government tonight bit- 
terly castigated the Soviet Union| 
as an aggressor. a treaty breaker 
and the master ot a Chinese Com- 
munist puppet regime threatening || 
the peace of the Far East. 

The official denunciation was 
read personally by George Yeh. 


‘Foreign Minister, to the Russian 


chargé d'affaires just 24 hours after 


Russia had officially recognized the || 


Communist “people's democracy” |' 
at Peiping and had severed rela- 
tions with the Canton Government. 

Summoning the Soviet diplomat, |, 
Vladimir Vayskov, to the Foreign) 
Office. Yeh informed him relations 
with the Soviet Union were ended. | 

Labeled Bogus Regime 

Yeh read to him a formal state- 
ment @é@tlaring that Russian rec- 
ognition of the “bogus regime” at 
Peiping was “not only an act of ag- 
gression against China, but also a 
threat to the peace and security ol 
the Far East.” 

Yeh stated that the recognition | 
was, however, only the natural } 
culmination of a long series of 
Russian violations of the Chinese- 
Soviet treaty of 1945 and was 


merely further evidence of Soviet! 


infringement on China's political 
independence and territorial in- 
tegrity. 

Russia, he said, was not only tear- 
ing the treaty to pieces but was 
committing an act contrary to the 
recognized principles of 
tional law and justice. 

Pact Gave Special Rights 
The 1945 treaty of friendship 


resulted from the American-Brit- } 


ish-Russian agreement at Yalta. It 
gave Russia many special rights in 
Manchuria. Chinese Nationalists 
frequently have complained, un- 
officially and semi-officially, that it 
was forced on China by the Big 
Three without advance notice and 
that Russia disregarded its pro- 
visions at her pleasure. 

“That the regime set up in 
'Peiping is Soviet-sponsored should 
be clear now to all the world,” de- 
clared Yeh's statement, “It is a pup- 
pet regime, forced upon the people 
against their free will, and_ its 
ideology is alien to Chinese civiliza- 
tion and the Chinese pattern ot 
life.”

PILOT, WANTS TO BECOME A JAPANESE GARRY DAVIS. | 

KAWATSU HAS PETITIONED THE GOVERNMENT FOR PERMISSION TO RENOUNCE HIS | 
JAPANESE CITIZENSHIP. 

"I WANT TO BECOME AN INTERNATIONAL CITIZEN LIKE THAT AMERICAN 
STUDENT," KAWATSU SAID. 

HE SAID HE HAD READ ABOUT DAVIS BUT COULD NOT REMEMBER HIS NAMEe 
(DAVIS RENOUNCED HIS AMERICAN CITIZENSHIP AND WENT TO EUROPE TO CAMPAIGN 
FOR WORLD PEACE.) 

"A THIRD WORLD WAR IS COMING,” KAWATSU SAID. "I DON'T WANT TO BE EN. 
IT. INSTEAD I WANT TO WORK FOR ETERNAL PEACE ON AN INTERNATIONAL 


PLANE."

COUIRED BY YOUNG COLLEGE STUDENTS HERE -=- THE KIND OF INTENSITY THAT

LAKE SUCCESS, OCTe4-(AP)=THE UNITED STATES REPORTED TO THR UNITED

COMMUNIST KASTERN EUROPE, 

AMERICAN DELEGATE BENJAMIN COHEN SAID THAT BULGARIA, WHERE 15 
PROTESTANT PASTORS WERE TRIED FAR TREASON LAST SPRING, TRIED ANOTHER 
GROUP OF PROTESTANTS IN JULY. 

COHEN SAID THR TRIAL WAS "THIS TIME IN SECRECY, PERHAPS FROM FEAR 
OF WORLDWIDE REACTION" SUCH AS FOLLOWED THE PREVIGUS CASES IN MARCH, 
ACCORDING TO RELIABLE REPORTS REACHING THE U.S. GOVERNMENT. 

THR AMERICAN DELEGATE SPOKE AT THE OUTSET OF DEBATE IN THE 
ASSEMBLY "S SPFCIAL POLITICAL COMMITTEE ON WESTERN CHARGES OF HUMAN 
RICHTS VIOLATIONS IN EX-ENEMY COUNTRIES NOW ALLIES OF SOVIET RUSSIA.

CARDINAL MINDSZENTY IS SERVING A LIFE TERM IN PRISON, AND 
NEW ACCUSATIONS OF SIMILAR NATURE AGAINST ROMANIA.

PASSENGERS.

PASSENGER AND POSSIBLE FURTHER PENALTIES.

THE SHIP, THE IRISH GOVERNMENT THEN WILL HAVE TO DECIDE THEIR FATEs

ITS FOUR PARLIAMENTARY SEATS IN.THIS.SUNDAY'S NATIONAL ELECTION-- 
AND THE ANTI*#COMMUNIST PARTIES HOPE IT DOES. 

THE RIGHT WING PEOPLES PARTY AND THE SOCIALISTS HAVE NOTHING BUT) 
ABUSE FOR THE COMMUNISTS, BUT THEY WANT THEM IN THE GOVERNMENT . 
"WHERE WE CAN KEEP OUR EYES ON THEM." 

IN 1945 THE PEOPLE'S PARTY WON 85 SEATS, THE SOCIALISTS 76 AND 
THE COMMUNISTS FOUR. SOME POLITICAL EXPERTS ARE PREDICCTING 
THE COMMUNISTS WILL DRAW A COMPLETE BLANK THIS SUNDAY. 

A SPOKESMAN FOR THE PEOPLE'S PARTY SAID TODAY IT WOULD BE 
"DISASTROUS" IF THE COMMUNISTS DO NOT SEAT AT LEAST ONE DEPUTY. 

"IF THEY HAVE NO REPRESENTATION IN THE GOVERNMENT THEY WILL GO 
UNDERGROUND AND PROBABLY CREATE A LOT OF UNREST IN THE COUNTRY," 

HE SAID. "SO LONG AS THEY ARE REPRESENTED IN PARLIAMENT THEY WILL 
HAVE TO STAY OUT IN THE OPEN. THAT IS WHAT WE WANT." 

A SOCIALIST LEADER EXPRESSED THE SAME VIEW, ADDING, “EVEN IF 

THEY GET THE SAME FOUR SEATS, THEY STILL WON'T BE STRONG ENOUGH

LEAST BEFORE ATOMIC FUEL THREATENS THE COAL INDUSTRY, AN ATOMIC i 
ENERGY COMMISSION ADVISOR SAID TODAY. 4 


PHILIP SPORN, PRESIDENT OF AMERICAN GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY, SAID) 
NUCLEAR FUEL WILL BE BURNED IN INDUSTRY ONE OF THESE DAYS, BUT IT 
WILL NOT BE A SIGNIFICANT COMPETITOR FOR COAL FOR A LONG TIME. 

SPORN DID NOT EXPECT RECENT REPORTS THAT RUSSIA HAD PRODUCED 
"AN ATOMIC EXPLOSION® WOULD HAVE ANY APPRECIABLE EFFECT ON THE 
PEACETIME ATOMIC EXPLORATION PROGRAM. 


THE UTILITIES HEAD RECENTLY WAS APPOINTED CHAIRMAN OF THE : 


ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON COOPERATION BETWEEN THE ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY | 
AND THE ATOMIC ENERGY COMMISSION. . 
HE TOLD THE NATIONAL COAL ASSOCIATION'S ANNUAL MEETING A LACK OF 
ESSENTIAL FACTS ON WHICH TO BASE ACCURATE ENGINEERING JUDGMENT LEAVES 

ESTIMATES ON ATOMIC FUEL LARGELY IN THE GUESSWORK CATEGORY. 

AND COSTS, HE SAID, WILL BE THE CRUX OF THE PROBLEM. 

THE COST OF A NUCLEAR POWER PLANT, SPORN SAID, HAS BEEN ESTIMATED 
ALL THE WAY FROM $140 TO $1,000 PER KILOWATT OF CAPACITY. 

(THIS COMPARED WITH AN AVERAGE COST OF $140 TO $200 A KILOWATT 


HYDRO PLANT'S COST IS A LITTLE MORE THAN THAT OF A STEAM GENERATING 
STATION.) 

SPORN SAID IF THE GUESS OF A COST AT THE LOWER LIMIT IS REALIZED 
OR BETTERED, ATOMIC POWER WILL HAVE GREAT SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC 
SIGNIFICANCE, 

EVEN IF THE COSTS CAN'T BE DROPPED TO OR NEAR THE LOWER 
LIMIT, HE ADDED, ATOMIC POWER STILL WILL HAVE SIGNIFICANCE IN PLACES 
REMOTE FROM ECONOMICAL SOURCES OF FUEL OR WATER POWER. 


AND IF COSTS STAY NEAR OR ABOVE THE VERY HIGH GUESSES, HE SAID, |) 
ATOMIC POWER IS UNLIKELY TO BE USED EXCEPT FOR MILITARY PURPOSES, i 


NAY) SAID NUCLEAR | 


WHERE COST CAN BE DISREGARDED. 

REGARDLESS OF HOW FAR OFF THE GUESSERS 
POWER IS STILL FAR AWAY.

HAVE A REACTOR PRODUCING ELECTRIC POWER. :

GENEVA (Monday), Oct. 
(AP) Mejor tariff reductions were | 


announced today by the. 31 nations| 
which took part in the world tariff 
conference at Afnecy, France, last 
summer. 

The list of tariff reducticns was 
an inch-thick volume laying down 
the miximum rates of import du y | 
on many thousands of different} 
items of international trade. The 
reducticns were agreed upon at the 
four-morth-long Annecy confer- 
ence of the’ founding members of 
the Geneva 1947 tariff agreement 
and 10 new countries acc 


The conference opened April 11]. 
and clcsed Aug. 27. It was the largz-/ 
est muttilateral tariff confab ever) 
held. It resu:ted in 147 bilateral tar- 
iff agreements between pairs of f 


countries. Under the most-favored-| 


nation principle of the Geneva 
agreement, any freezing or reduc-, 
tion of tariffs agreed in one of the! 
bilatera: agreements is automati-. 
cally applied to the exports of all 
the other member states of the 
agreement. 

Not As Far-Reaching 
In volume of trade affected, the 
\nnecy conference was not nearly»! 
far-reaching as the original | 
Geneva tariff conference of 1947, 
when the original 23 member states 
of the agreement negotiated tariff 
concessions among themselves. It 
was estimated that the 1947 aon- 
ference affected more than 70 per 
cent of the world’s total volume of 
trade, 

The Annecy conference, on the 
other hand, covered negotiations 
only between the original members| 
and the ten new members as well! 
as among the newcomers theme! 
selves. It thus covered less than 
ten per cent of the world’s trade. 

Nevertheless, the Annecy cone 
‘ference considerably extended the! 
effectiveness of the Geneva pen 
ment. A third round of traiff talks 
is due to be held next year. at 
which some of the major trading 
nations still outside the agreement, 


including A rgentina, Mexico and

WASHINGTON, Oct, 13 (AP)— 


Louis E. Denfeld, Chief of Naval 


Operations, as part of his state-\ 
ment to the House Armed Services |y 


Committee: 

It bears repetition for me to 
say that I am for unification. Be- 
cause there seems to be so many 
different definitions and _ inter- 
pretations of this term ‘‘unifica- 
tion,’’ I will again state my un- 


derstanding that unification con- 


templates basically a coordina-° 


. tion of effort. It does not mean 


tion. 


or elimina- 


merger, absorption, 
unification 


Furthermore, 


should not mean that two serv- 


ices can control a third. Up to 


now there have been many in- 


stances in which that has hap- 


pened. 


While there is a law saying tha 


_ there shall be naval aviation and 
there shall be a Marine Corps, 
and although there have been 


public utterances from our sister 


_ services that there shall be naval 
_ aviation and a Marine Corps, in 


the councils of the Department 
of Defense the opposite view is 


often evident. 


Furthermore, regardless of 
laws intended to preserve naval 
aviation and the Marine Corps, if 
the funds to sustain them are 
choked off or the composition 


| of the Navy is determined by a 


2-to-1 vote regardless of funds 
available, then naval aviation 


and the Marines will be put out 
_ of business as surely as if there 


_ Army and Air Force have disap- 


had been no law. 


In numerous instances the 


proved proposals advanced by 


_ the Navy pertaining to naval avi- 


ation and the Marine 


ign 


Corps. 
There is no intention to impugn 
the motives of any person in this 
respect; rather, it arises from 
lack of study or lack of experi- 
ence in naval matters, or both. 
Nevertheless, these disapprovals 
constitute a pattern which I can- 
ore. 

The instability which I have 
described as a result of continu- 
ing efforts to make basic changes 
in the roles and missions of the 


_ armed services seriously jeopard- 
izes efficient planning and admin- 


istration. 
I can understand the view that 


_ it is regrettable the basic differ- 


_ to our national security; 


ences revealed in these hearings 
have been aired in public, I be- 
lieve, however, it would have 
been immeasurably more regret- 
table had these issues remained 
hidden and a false sense of se- 
curity been permitted to prevail. 
This is so: , 


Because the issues are so vital

ae

mation presented by Admiral 


unification is more injurious than 
no unification at all; and 
Because, under our system of 


~ Government it is the people who 


are the final judges of the stew- 
ardship of Government officials. 
As I see this hearing, it began 


on the note of maladministration 
by high Government officials. 


_ That I abhor. I am deeply grati- 
| fied that it proved to be a sour

Because the core of the hearing 


was only natural that the Navy, 
which is charged by law with an 
important role in military air 


| power, should be required to pre- 
_ sent its views. Furthermore, be- 


cause of our vital role in military 
air power, it would have been 
reprehensible, under the concept 
of democracy, had we not ex- 
pressed our frank views. 

I have summarized the various 
respects in which the armed 


- forces are not now following the 
- spirit and pursuing the purpose 


\ of unification. The fault is not 


with the law or its intent but is 
the fact that the law has not yet 


- begun to function as the Congress 


intended. 
What does the Navy propose 
should now be done? 
First—Expedite the report of 
the Weapons Evaluation Group in 
order to determine the military 


worth of the B-36. 

Second—Literally support the 
National Security Act and the 
Key West Agreement on roles 


and missions of the armed forces. 

Third—Support the principle 
that each service within budget- 
ary limitations be permitted to 
design and develop its own weap- 
ons. 

Fourth—Provide the Navy ade- 
quate and appropriate represen- 
tation in key positions within the 


- Department of Defense. 


Fifth—Limit the scope of activ- 
ities of the Joint Chiefs of Staff 
to those specifically mentioned in 
the National Security Act. 

Sixth—In the present stage of 
unification, it must be recognized 
that the views of a particular 
service are entitled to predomi- 
nant weight in the determination 


| of the forces needed by that serv- 


ice to fulfill its missions. 

The accomplishment of these 
points will not in itself solve all 
our national security problems. 
It will, however, go far toward 
providing a framework which will 
permit a unified approach to the 


grave problems of national secu- be

LAKE SUCCESS, OCT 14=C(AP)-CARLOS P.ROMULO, PRESIDENT OF THE UNLIED 
NATIONS ASSEMBLY, SAID TODAY THE U.Ne IS CHANGING FROM THE ROLE OF 
PEACE*MAINTAINER TO THAT OF PEACE-MAKER. 

HIS STATEMENT IS PUBLISHED IN A SPECIAL ISSUE OF THE UNITED 
NATIONS BULLETIN, OFFICIAL BI-WEEKLY MAGAZINE OF THE UeNe THE ISSUE 
IS DEDICATED TO UNITED NATIONS DAY, OCT. 24, WHEN PRESIDENT TRUMAN 
COMES TO NEW YORK TO LAY THE CORNERSTONE OF THE NEW U.NeHEADQUARTERS 
BUILDING IN EAST SIDE, MIDTOWN NEW YORK.

WROTE, “THE UNITED NATIONS. WAS NOT INTENDED TO. MAKE) THE PEACE BUT 
ONLY TO MAINTAIN IT.® 

"EVENTS HAVE ALL BUT ERASED THAT FINE DISTINCTION,®* HE ADDED. 

ROMULO SAID THE RECORD OF THE U.Ne IN ITS FIRST FOUR YEARS IS 


GOOD--EVERYTHING CONSIDERED. 
"IT MIGHT HAVE BEEN BETTER IF THERE HAD BEEN A LITTLE MORE GOOD 


WILL. LESS SUSPICION AND ANIMOSITY, MORE COOPERATION AND UNITY OF r 
PURPOSE AMONG THE MEMBER STATES--ESPECIALLY THE BIG POWERS WHO 2 


HAVE THE STRENGTH TO MAKE THE PEACE AND THE MEANS, IF THEY SHOULD WILL 
IT, TO HARNESS EVEN THE MIGHTY ATOM TO THE SERVICE. OF MAN.®* 
ROMULO SAID THE PEOPLES OF THE WORLD, IN THEIR ESTIMATES OF THE UeNe 


SUCCESS OR FAILURE, SHOULD ASK THEMSELVES WHAT THEY HAVE DONE AND H 
WHAT THEY HAVE FAILED TO DO FOR THE U.N. , + i949 i:

OF THE PROBLEMS AND CONFLICTS THAT BLOCK THE ROAD TO UNDERSTANDING, y 


AGREEMENT AND CO-OPERATION AMONG THE NATIONS.

ENERGY. A SPECIAL RESPONSIBILITY FALLS UPON THE BIG POWERS IN : 4 er 
THIS CRUCIAL PROBLEM, BUT ITS JUST AND EFFECTIVE SOLUTION IS THE | 
CONCERNOF ALL. IT IS MY HOPE THAT PROGRESS TOWARDS AGREEMENT WILL us V

THE HAGUE, Oct. 15 UP).—Co-, 
lombia today took its quarrel with,

political refugees, to the Interna- 
tional Court of Justice. 

Colombia is demanding safe 
conduct for the Peruvian Apra 
party leader, Victor Raul Haya de 
la Torre, who took refage In the 
Colombian Embassy Lima oy. 
Jan. 1 after an attempted military 
coup failed, 

' Peru has charged that Haya de 
la Torre is not a political refugee) 
jbut is guilty of “ordinary crimes” 
in leading an abortive revolt at’ 
Callao on Oct. 3, 1948. Peru has 
refused to grant him permission 
to leave the country, as Colom- 
‘bia has asked. 

| Colombia says the refusal by! 
Peru to grant Haya De la Torre) 
isafe conduct jeopardizes the im- 
portant “right of asylum” clause 
‘of the 1928 Havana Convention. 

The International Court regis- 

try will announce officially on 
Monday the submision of the case 
but no date has yet been fixed for 
hearings.

Pennsylvania's ‘Flying 


Believed Lo Be Furn 


An army officer said today a dough- 
nut-shaped disk found near here 
that revived “flying saucer’e reports 
was the top of a hot air furnace. 

“It was somebedy's joke.” said} 
Major George Stephens, of the; 
near-by Susquehanna Army  sub- 
depot, after examining the device. | 
| “It is the top of a hot air furnace} 
which somebody cut off with an 
lacetylene torch,” Major Stephens) 
said. He made it plain that he was’ 
voicing a personal opinjon, 

The disk was recovered from the! 
town park at Laperte.Pa., about 25: 
miles. gortheast of here. | 

Say It Fell Flaming | 

Witnesses said the disk fell flam- 
ing from the sky last August 5 and 
landed in the park where it burned} 
a 10-foot swath in the grass. 

The witnesses said several explo-} 
sions took place as the disk de- 
scended toward the ground. 

M. R. Stepp, county survevor 
and one of the witnesses, said the 
doughnut-shaped disc was illumi- 


‘nated when traveling through the} 
air. 

“The device continued to burn 
for approximately 15 minutes 
after it had landed,” Stepp said, 
adding: 

“Hot solder poured from the 
device after it landed. 

“No one heard a motor of any 
planes at the time the contraption 
landed.” 

50 Report Seeing Disk 

Some 50 persons reported seeing 
the device flying and burning. 

The disk is shaped like a dough- 
nut and is a little larger than an 
automobile inner tube. A protrud- 
ing round cylinder on one side} 
contains dials. Residents who ex-| 
amined the contrivance said it} 
contained what appeared to be} 
radio equipment in its hollow in-| 
terior. 

The disk lav in the park area} 
\for more than two months before &amp; 
lthe Army learned of its presence 
jand took it over for study. :

politan Training Center, Inc., of| 
,;New York city. and the Michigan

enforcing a regulation it issued in

out of the GI bill's provision that 


payment ‘for veterans tuition 
under the measure shall be at 
“customary” rates. 
VA Contention Upheld 
The regulation pointed out that 
cchools established after the GI 
bill became effective June 22, 1944, 
could not be considered as having} 
customary tuition rates and there- 
fore must show that tuition charges 
are fair and reasonable. 
Judge MeGuire upheld the VA 
contention that the Federal Gov- 
ernment may not be sued for in-f 
junctive relief without its consent 
that the regulations are valid. 
A VA spokesman said that, since} 
the test suits were brought, con- 
tracts with new schools had in-§ 
cluded an escape clause to permit f 
the schools to set “customary” 
rates in event the cases were} 
decided against the Veterans Ad-/ 
ministration.

NEW YORK, OCT 17-CAP)-A SCHOOLBOY ASKED INDIA’S PRIME MINISTER 
JAWAHARLAL NEHRU TODAY "WOULD YOUR COUNTRY FIGHT WITH THE UNITED 
STATES IF WE WENT TO WAR WITH RUSSIA?" 

"IT IS BEST THAT THERE BE NO WAR AGAIN," NEHRU REPLIED WITH A 
SMILE "BUT IF WAR COMES AND ENDANGERS THE FREEDOM OF A COUNTRY, IT) 
JOULD "HAVE TO DEFEND ITSELF.* 

THE INTERVIEW WAS AN IMPROMPTU ONE IN WHICH A GROUP OF ABOUT 
20 SCHOOL CHILDREN BOMBARDED THE PRIME MINISTER WITH QUESTIONS. 


kg 


"I MUST SAY YOUR QUESTIONS ARE VERY BRIGHT QUESTIONS,* NEHRU SAID« 


"ASK YOUR QUESTIONS," HE INVITED THE YOUNGSTERS WHO HAD GREETED 
HIM. AN INDIAN GIRL IN THE GROUP HANDED HIM A BOUQUET. OTHERS 
HANDED HIM A SCROLL LETTERED BY THEIR GROUP. | 

HE SIGNED AUTOGRAPH BOOKS AND AUTOGRAPH PICTURES OF HIMSELF. 
THEN THE QUESTIONS STARTED. THE YOUNGSTERS WERE TOO EXCITED TO 
PAY ANY ATTENTION TO REPORTERS WHO WANTED TO KNOW THEIR NAMES. 

"WHAT IS THE WORST PROBLEM IN INDIA TODAY?" A LITTLE GIRL INQUIRED. 

"POVERTY," CAME THE UNHESITATING REPLY. “WE MUST HAVE FOOD FOR 
OUR PEOPLE." 

THE CHILDREN ASKED NEHRU WHETHER HIS PEOPLE STILL FOLLOWED THE 
TEACHINGS OF MOHANDAS GANDHI. HE-TOLD THEM THAT NOT ALL OF THEM 
FOLLOWED THE TEACHINGS IMPLICITLA ‘BUT (TRAY) THEY REVERED THE SLAIN 
HINDU LEADER. 

HE WAS ASKED BY ANOTHER BOY HOW THE INDIANS FEEL TOWARD THE 
BRITISH. 

"THEIR RULE IN INDIA WAS OBJECTED TO STRONGLY, BUT INDIVIDUAL 
ENGLISHMEN WE LIKE," NEHRU SAID. 

HE TOLD THE CHILDREN HOW ELEPHANTS AND CAMELS ARE USED IN INDIA 
TO DO HEAVY WORK AND SOMETIMES FOR PLEASURE RIDING. | :

| world’—and he counselled them to

work.” 

Top Navy admirals have accus- 
ed the Army and Air Force of 
“ganging up” under the unified) 
defense setup to deprive the Navy 
of its offensive power. Generals 
in turn have lashed back at the 
Navy leadership. 

Mark Clark Testifies

committee today, Gen. Mark Clark

in unification of the armed forces.

3,000 Homeless 
In Ch Fire 
Chungking, Oct. 22 (#)—Fire 


raged through Chungking’s pover- 
ty-stricken Changpei district today, 
leaving more than 3,000 homeless. 
No casu alties were reported in the 
city’s fourth bad blaze since Sep- 
2. 

Two employés of a tobacco dry- 
ing shop, where the fire was be- 
lieved to have started, were ar- 
rested on charges of negligence. 

Lack of fire-fighting apparatus 
and the tardy arrival of fireboats 
on the Chialiang Riyer gave the 
fire. free rein. Only frenzied tear- 
ing down of buildings to create fire 
lanes limited the flames. Some 217 
homes were reported destroyed.

CURRENT ARAB LEAGUE COUNCIL MEETING, REPORTEDLY WERE MADE AT 
BEHIND=THE@SCENES CONFERENCES LAST NIGHT. 

ONLY TWO MAJOR ISSUES NOW REMAIN BEFORE THE COUNCIL: 

1=-THE QUESTION OF A COMMON ECONOMIC POLICY TOWARD ISRAEL, 
INCLUDING A POSSIBLE BOYCOTT OF ISRAELI PRODUCTS. 

Q-=INTERNAL REORGANIZATION OF THE LEAGUE SECRETARIAT, ON 
WHICH IRAQ IS INSISTING. 

THE INFORMANTS SAID AGREEMENT IS LIKELY ON THE FIRST QUESTION. 


THEY ALSO BELIEVE ANY EFFORT BY IRAQ TO FORCE REPLACEMENT OF THE 
PRESENT PERMANENT SECRETARIAT BY A COUNCIL INCLUDING A REPRESENTATIVE 
FROM EACH ARAB STATE WILL PROBABLY FAIL, DUE TO SHARP OPPOSITION FROM) 


EGYPT AND SAUDI ARABIA. 

THE DECISION TO DISCONTINUE DISCUSSIONS OF IRAQI-SYRIAN 
UNION CAME AFTER SYRIA, IRAQ, AND HASHEMITE JORDAN INSISTED IT 
WAS AN INTERNAL MATTER FOR THE TWO COUNTRIES TO DECIDE, THESE 


SOURCES SAID. 


IRAQ AND HASHEMITE JORDAN, IN OPPOSING THE INTERNATIONLIZATION OF 


JERUSALEM, WERE SAID TO HAVE INVITED THAT SUCH A STEP WOULD 


PROVIDE THE JEWS WITH AN OPPORTUNITY TO INDIRECTLY WIN CONTROL OF THE 


ENTIRE HOLY CITY THROUGH INFILTRATION IN THE U.N. ADMINISTRATION. 
THE OTHER ARAB STATES FAVORED INTERNATIONALIZATION. TROOPS 

OF HASHEMITE JORDAN STILL OCCUPY THE ANCIENT PORTION OF JERUSALEM. 
SINCE UNDER THE ARAB LEAGUE CONSTITUTION, A MAJORITY DECISION 

BINDS ONLY THE POWERS VOTING FOR THE PROPOSAL, IT WAS DECIDED TO 


LEAVE THE QUESTION OF INTERNALIZATION WITH THE INDIVIDUAL STATES, —_ 
RATHER THAN OPENLY SHOW ARAB DISUNITY ON THE PROPOSAL. ~~ Y 7)

AUSTIN CAME HERE FROM THE U.N. ASSEMBLY IN NEW YORK TO SPEAK AT 
A CITY-WIDE CONFERENCE SPONSORED BY THE U.N. COMMITTEE OF THE BUFFALO 
COUNCIL ON WORLD AFFAIRS TO MARK OBSERVANCE OF U.N. WEEK. 

IN A PREPARED SPEECH, AUSTIN REFERRED TO THE RESOLUTION INTRODUCED 
IN THE U.N. ASSEMBLY BY THE CHINESE NATIONALIST GOVERNMENT 
CHARGING RUSSIA WITH VIOLATING HER TREATY OF FRIENDSHIP BY AIDING THE 


CHINESE REDS. 
HE SAID THE ASSEMBLY WOULD HAVE GREAT DIFFICULTY IN DEALING WITH 


THE QUESTION. 

*WE CANNOT EXPECT THAT THAT COURSE OF EVENTS (CIN CHINA) WILL BE 
REVERSED OR HALTED MERELY BY A PRONOUNCEMENT OF THE ASSEMBLY, * HE . 
ADDED. 

"WHAT MIGHT PERHAPS EMERGE FROM THE CONSIDERATION OF THIS CASE. 
WOULD BE A REAFFIRMATION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF CERTAIN BASIC 
PRINCIPLES OF THE CHARTER AS THEY APPLY’ TO CHINA'S INDEPENDENCE FROM 


FOREIGN DOMINATION AND TO THE RIGHT OF CHINA'S PEOPLE TO CHOOSE THEIR | |AHE 


OWN POLITICAL INSTITUTIONS. SUCH A STATEMENT BY THE ASSEMBLY COULD 
HAVE A SIGNIFICANT LONG-TERM EFFECT IN DEMONSTRATING TO THE CHINESE 
PEOPLE THAT THE UNITED NATIONS HAS A VITAL CONCERN IN THEIR WELFARE 


AND THEIR DESTINY." 
FOR THE FIRST TIME, AUSTIN OFFICIALLY TIPPED THE UeS. HAND IN 


ASSEMBLY BATTLE OVER THE SOVIET DEMAND FOR A FIVE-POWER 
ACT. 

AUSTIN SAID THE U.S. AND BRITAIN WILL PROPOSE TO THE ASSEMBLY A 
RESOLUTION TO *SET FORTH IN CLEAR, UNMISTAKABLE TERMS THE ESSENTIALS 
FOR PEACEFUL COOPERATION AMONG NATIONS." 

HE DESCRIBED RUSSIA*S PROPOSAL AS AN OLIVE BRANCH BRISTLING 
"WITH THE POISONOUS THORNS OF PROPAGANDA.® 

“FOR THE FIRST TIME,* HE DECLARED, *THE SOVIET GOVERNMENT HAS 
SHIFTED FROM LEVELING ACCUSATIONS AT. "CERTAIN CIRCLES* AND SPECIFIC 
INDIVIDUALS AND HAS DIRECTLY CHARGED THAT THE. GOVERNMENTS OF THE 


UNITED STATES, THE UNITED KINGDOM AND THOSE OF OTHER UNNAMED COUNTRIES 


ARE PREPARING FOR A NEW WAR, ENCOURAGING WAR PROPAGANDA, ORGANIZING 
MILITARY BLOCS AND PURSUING OTHER AGGRESSIVE AIMS." 


AUSTIN OUTLINED MANY OF THE ISSUES BEFORE THE CURRENT U.N. ASSEMBLY 


AND ALSO MENTIONED MANY OF THE QUESTIONS SOLVED OR HELPED THROUGH 


U.N. INTERVENTION,

Mr. Truman’s Address 


President Romulo, Mr. Lie, | 
Governor Dewey, Mayor O’Dwyer, 
distinguished representatives and © 
fellow-guests: 


We have come together today to 
lay the cornerstone of the per- 
manent headquarters of. the 
United Nations. These are the 
most important buildings in the 
world, for'they are the center of 
man‘s hope for peace and a bet- | 
ter life. This is the place where 
the nations of the world. wi 
work together. to make. that-hi 
a reality. 

This occasion is a source of 
special pride to the people of the 
United States. We are deeply 
conscious of the honor of having 
the permanent headquarters of 
the United Nations in this coun- 
try, At the same time, we know 
how important it is that the peo- 
ple of other nations should come 
to know at first hand the work 
of this world organization. We 
consider it appropriate, therefore, 
that the United Nations should 
hold meetings from time to time 
in other countries when that can 
be done. For the United Nations 
must draw its inspiration from 
the people of every land; it must. 
be truly representative of and 


responsive to the peoples of the 
world whom it was created to 
serve.

| LONDON, Oct. 24 Ph—George 
Strauss, Minister of Supply, told 
the House of*Commons today that 
dealings in tin would be re- 
sumed on Nov. 15. The Govern-; 
ment thus will abandon its war- 
time policy of bulk buying and 
selling. 

|| Mr. Strauss said that the Lon- 
'|don Metal Exchange, closed during 
the war, would reopen but would 
jnot, however, deal in copper, lead 
and zinc.

MEXICO CITY, “Oct. 25- (AP) 4 
What should you do if an atomil 
bomb hits your town? | 

The safest thing is to stay in} 
doors, wherever you are, unless 
there is specific reason for evacua4 
tion of the area. Turn on the radio’ 
if there is .any current, and be} 
ready to fight local fires and follow? 
instructions. | 

This was the answer given to-| 
day by Maj. Albert J. Bauer of the! 
U.S. Army Surgeon of-| 
fice, in a report before the 12th endl 
ternatinoal Congress on Military) 
Medicine and Pharmacy. He was!

John army | 
medical center. The report was} 
based on a study of the explosions) 
at Hiroshiraa, Nagasaki and Bikini. 

“Atomic Fears” Battled 


It tries to get rid of “atomic neu-| 
rosis,” or fear of the unknown pro- 
duced in some people by the atomic} 


bomb. 

To begin with, Bauer says, your: 
chance against the atomic bomb is] 
better than you might think. 

If you are four miles or more 
from an explsoion your chances of | 
escaping death or injury are al- | 
most perfect. 

From there on toward the cen-| 
ter your chances drop off rapidly, | 
though from a hilf mile to a mile | 
and half from the blast center the | 
chance is about 50-50 that you will 
come out alive. 

Vithin a half mile ‘radius there 
will be almost complete destruc- 
tion and fatalities will be very close 
to 100 per cent. Relief workers are 
advised to write you off as a “total 
loss” if you are in that area. 
The report says preparation and | 
organization beforehand is of the 
greatest importance in holding cas- 
ualties to a minimum and reestab-

LONDON, OCT. 26=(AP)=BRITAIN AGREED TODAY TO GIVE MORE 
FREEDOM TO THE GOLD COAST, ITS STRATEGIC WEST AFRICAN COLONY. 
BUT THE GOVERNMENT REFUSED TO GRANT AL THE INDEPENDENCE THE 
GOLD COAST'S 4,000,000 AFRICANS HAVE DEMANDED. 
COLONIAL SECRETARY ARTHUR CREECH JONES ANNOUNCED 
APPROVAL OF A PLAN WHICH WOULD SET UP A 12=MAN *CABINET® 
TO TOP AN EXPANDED PARLIAMENT. ELECTION OF THE LEGISLATURE 
WOULD BE INDIRECT. 
HE REFUSED, ON BEHALF OF THE BRITISH GOVERNMENT, TO 
ACCEPT THE AFRICANS’ DEMANDS FOR A TWO-CHAMBER INSTEAD OF A 


ONE=CHAMBER PARLIAMENT; AND FOR MAKING THE CABINET RESPONSIBLE 
Vg GERMAN C 
TODAY HF 


PARLIAMENT 
INSTEAD, HE INSISTED ON A ONE*CHAMBER PARLIAMENT AND AM 


MAKING THE CABINET ANSWERABLE TO THE COLONIAL GOVERNOR WHOM HE 
APPOINTS HIMSELF. 

THE AFRICANS' DEMANDS WERE FRAMED BY AN ALL=BLACK 39=-MAN 
COMMISSION ASSIGNED LAST YEAR TO WORK OUT A NEW CONSTITUTION FOR THE 
COLONY. CREECH JONES' COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION'S REPORT WERE MADE 
IN THE FORM OF A DISPATCH TO THE GOLD COAST ADMINISTRATION. BOTH 
DOCUMENTS WERE PRESENTED TO THE HOUSE OF COMMONS TODAY. 

RESPONSIBLE INFORMANTS SAID BRITAIN'S DIFFERENCES WITH THE 
COMMISSION MIGHT TOUCH OFF A NEW CONFLICT BETWEEN THE GOLD COASTERS 


AND THE BRITISH. 
THE INFORMANTS SAID BRITISH TROOPS FROM GIBRALTAR WOULD BE FLOWN 


IN TO HELP KEEP ORDER, IF NEEDED. | 

THE COMMISSION’S INQUIRY FOLLOWED LONGTIME ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL 
UNREST IN THE RICH BRITISH COLONY. THE UNREST CULMINATED IN 
EXTENSIVE RIOTS IN FEBRUARY, 1948, AT ACCRA, THE COLONY'S CAPITAL. 
RIOTING AFRICANS AT THE TIME BESIEGED THE GOVERNOR IN HIS HOME 
FOR SEVERAL DAYS. TROOPS WERE CALLED OUT. A FEW AFRICANS WERE 
KILLED IN SUBSEQUENT SHOOTINGS. 

THE BRITISH CHARGED THE DISTURBANCES HAD BEEN INSPIRED BY 
COMMUNIST AGENTS SEEKING TO SET UP A SOVIET EAST AFRICAN STATE.

ARE LEARNING TO TAKE WAR IN THEIR STRIDE. 

THESE WERE CONCLUSIONS IN A REPORT ON "WAR PSYCHOSES® PREPARED FOR |

MEDICINE AND PHARMACY. DR. Je PARAIRE, MEDICAL COMMANDER AT VAL=DE-

DR. PARAIRE SAYS NOT ONLY ARE THE MENTAL DIFFICULTIES OF 
THE MODERN SOLDIER MORE COMPLEX, BUT THERE ARE MORE OF THEM. 

HE SAYS THERE WERE THREE TIMES AS MANY SOLDIERS IN WORLD WAR TWO AS 
IN WORLD WAR ONE, AND TEN TIMES AS MANY WERE IN HOSPITALS WITH 
NERVOUS COMPLAINTS. 
HE ADDS: *THE SECOND WORLD WAR SHOWS THE CURIOUS RESULT OF AN | 
INCREASE OF MENTAL DISORDERS AMONG ARMIES AND A DECREASE AMONG THE 
CIVIL POPULATION.®

A UNITED NATIONS FIELD SERVICE TODAY AS A “SUBTLE AMERICAN SCHEME TO 
TURN THE UNITED NATIONS INTO AN OBEDIENT WEAPON OF ITS OWN SELFISH 
POLICY."* |

HE RECALLED THAT THE UNITED STATES SENATE RECENTLY AUTHORIZED THE 
PRESIDENT TO MAKE AVAILABLE UP TO 1,000 MEN TO THE UNITED NATIONS ANY 
TIME IT REQUESTED SUCH A FORCE. 

"WHO," HE ASKED, “MADE ANY SUCH REQUEST OF THE UNITED STATES?® 

THE FIELD SERVICE IS A WATERED DOWN VERSION OF SECRETARY@GENERAL 
TRYGVE LIE'S PROPOSAL FOR A SMALL UNITED NATIONS ARMED SERVICE. 

IT WOULD BE LIMITED TO 300 MEN, ARMED ONLY WITH REVOLVERS, AND USED 
PRIMARILY FOR SUCH DUTIES AS RADIO OPERATING AND CHAUFFEURING FOR 
UNITED NATIONS MISSIONS IN PLACES LIKE PALESTINE, INDONESIA AND GREECE. 


TSARAPKIN DENOUNCED WHAT HE CALLED AN ATTEMPT TO ESTABLISH A PRIVATE 


U.N. ARMY BY DISGUISING IT UNDER THE NAME "FIELD SERVICE." 

"THIS DECEIVES NO ONE," HE SAID. “THIS FIELD SERVICE WILL BE A 
TOOL OF THE ANGLO-AMERICAN POLICY WHICH SEEKS TO BY-PASS THE SECURITY 
COUNCIL." 

THE RUSSIANS HAVE CHARGED IN ALL DEBATES ON SETTING UP THE SERVICE 
THAT IT WOULD ESTABLISH A POWERFUL MILITARY ARM OF THE UNITED NATIONS 
NOT SUBJECT TO THE SECURITY COUNCIL. A RUSSIAN VETO IN THE SECURITY 
COUNCIL COULD BLOCK ANY ACTION NOT TO RUSSIA'S LIKING. THEY CLAIM 
THAT THE WEST'S SO=CALLED "AUTOMATIC MAJORITY" IN THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY 
WOULD ENABLE THOSE POWERS TO ASSIGN U.N. MILITARY UNITS, NOT SUBJECT

Mother F alls Dead 
As She Finds Son 


Sees Lost Sailor in Asylum 


After World-Wide Hunt 


Africa, Oct! 
28 ().—A.woman-who had traced 
her missing sailor son around the 


- globe fell dead of shock here when) 


she faced him. The story was re-| 
lated today by her husband at her’ 
funeral. 

Mrs. R. Levi, of Aden, kissed her 
nineteen-year-old son good bye 
early in World War II when he left; 
to join the Royal Navy. After sev-| 
eral months she was advised that! 
his ship was torpedoed—all hands| 
lost. 
She refused to believe her oie 
dead. She wandered through Medi-| 
terranean ports seeking him. She 


visited Britain, the United States) 


and Australia in the search. At} 
one time she spent eleven days) 
and nights of terror and starvation |: 
in an open boat. 

- Then in an asylum at Observa- 


tory, near Capetown, she found her” 


son. The war victim was a human 
wreck who could only mutter 
“Shalom, shalom” — the Hebrew) 


word for “peace.” 
She looked at him, crumpled to 


‘the floor, and died.

WARM@HEARTED AND LIKEABLE, BUT THAT HE WON'T HITCH INDIA‘S WAGON TO AN

"WHY SHOULD WE, OF OUR OWN FREE WILL, TIE OURSELVES UP AND MAKE

MEANWHILE THE GUESSING CONTINUES. WHAT WOULD INDIA'S RECOGNITION 

HINA IMPLY? WOULD IT MEAN MORE THAN RECOGNITION BY BRITAIN WOULD 
MEAN? THE QUESTIONS GO ON FROM THERE, ENDLESSLY.

PEOPLE FROM TYING TOO CLOSELY TO THE RUSSIANS. HE KNOWS THE STORY OF 
MARSHAL TITO OF YUGO SLAVIA. |

AGAINST POVERTY AND MISTREATMENT THAN AN EMBRACING OF COMMUNIST

THAN IN THE POLITICS OF THE FELLOW WHO PROMISES TO LEAD THEM TO 
IT, IN NEHRU'S VIEW N HIS OWN COUNTRY HE HAS SEEN INDIANS CRYING 
COMMUNIST SLOGANS WHO DOUB 3TLESS WERE TOO IGNORANT TO UNDERSTAND WHAT 
COMMUNISM MEANS. HE FEELS IT WAS THE MEN WHO TAUGHT THE SLOGANS WHO

AND THE LIKE" BUT NOT ANY SOMETHING-FOR-NOTHING DEALS.

MANILA, Oct. 30.—President 
‘Elpidio Quirino announced today

February. President Quirino said”

Even . ssuming brilliant success 
in overcoming the dollar deficit 
in the next two years, the end 
of ERP in 1952 will at best leave 
Europe in only a precarious bal- 
ance with the dollar area. Mone- 
tary reserves will be inadequate, 
and it is plain that dollar short- 
ages will recur in one country or 
another the first time the Euro- 
pean economy is_ subjected to 
a pressure. In the absence 


integration, nations would 
each separately try to protect 
their dollar reserves. They 


would attempt to earn dollars 
from each other by restricting 
imports. The vicious cycle of eco- 
nomic nationalism would again 
be set in motion. 

The consequences would be the 
cumulative narrowing of mar- 
kets, the further growth of high 
cost protected industries, the 
mushrooming of restrictive con- 
trols, and the shrinkage of trade 
into the primitive pattern of bi- 
lateral barter. 

This course spells disaster for 
nations and poverty for peoples. 
This is why integration is not just 
- ideal. It is a practical neces- 
sity, 

This being so, it is your job to 
» devise and put into effect your 
own program to accomplish this 
purpose—just as it was your re- | Ba. 
sponsibility, which you carried | : 
out so ably, to take Secretary | . 
Marshall’s original suggestion and | 
give it life and breath. 

May I say I am, of course, quite 
aware that some of the concepts | 
I am here discussing are familiar 
to you. They have been mentioned 
| by numerous Ministers in conver- 
sations with me. I have “been |. 
gratified that several of these | 
ideas are included in a paper pre- | 
sented by one of the Ministers. 

In a program designed to ac- . 
complish effective and lasting in- | &gt; 
tegration, certain fundamental | 
requirements suggest themselves. |? 
First, means must be found to 
bring about a substantial measure 
of coordination of national fiscal | 
and monetary policies, Trade and | 
payments cannot lon, continue | 
free among countries in which | ; 
there are widely divergent de- ' 
grees of inflationary, or defla- | 
tionary, pressure. The develop- | 
ment of such differences in | 
financial pressures among differ- | 
ent countries will inevitably force | 
the reimposition of restrictive | 
controls, 

Unless individual countries ac- | 
cept the necessity for some co- | 
ordination of domestic financial | 
policies, the prospects for elimi- 
nating even the most restrictive 
types of controls over internation-\|, 
al trade will be dim indeed. Co- | 
ordination of these vital national 


~~ 


there will 


policies need not result in identity 


of policy. Coordination need only | 


go so far as to insure that poli- 
cies will not diverge so drastically 
as to break down the whole 
structure of European unity; but 
it must go at least that far, 


Exchange Rate Changes 


Another essential of your plan, 
I believe, is that it should provide 


means for necessary exchange | 


rate adjustments, subject, of 
course, to the general supervision 
of the International Monetary 
Fund, where these are the only 


feasible alternatives to imposing | 


direct exchange controls within 
Europe. This is necessary because 
be occasions when, 
either for reasons of policy or as 
as result of circumstances beyond 


the control of government, prices | 


and costs in one country will di- 
verge from those in other coun- 
tries too far to be brought into 
line through internal financial 
measures alone. 

Even when effective means are 
found to coordinate financial poli- 
cies and to promote needed ex- 
change rate changes, 


turbances in the flow of trade 
and payments between countries. 
Their whole impact should not be
